In [[mathematics]], the '''Jacobian ideal''' or '''gradient ideal''' is the [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] generated by the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of a function or [[germ (mathematics)|function germ]].
Let <math>\mathcal{O}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> denote the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of [[Smoothness|smooth functions]] in <math>n</math> variables and <math> f</math> a function in the ring.  The Jacobian ideal of <math> f</math> is
:<math> J_f := \left\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \right\rangle. </math>

== Relation to deformation theory ==
In [[deformation theory]], the deformations of a [[hypersurface]] given by a [[polynomial]] <math>f</math> is classified by the ring<math display=block>
\frac{\mathbb{C}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]}{(f) + J_f}.</math>
This is shown using the [[Kodaira–Spencer map]].

== Relation to Hodge theory ==
In [[Hodge theory]], there are objects called real [[Hodge structure|Hodge structures]] which are the data of a real vector space <math>H_\mathbb{R}</math> and an increasing [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] <math>F^\bullet</math> of <math>H_\mathbb{C} = H_\mathbb{R}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}</math> satisfying a list of compatibility structures. For a smooth projective variety <math>X</math> there is a canonical Hodge structure.

=== Statement for degree d hypersurfaces ===
In the special case <math>X</math> is defined by a homogeneous degree <math>d</math> polynomial <math>f \in \Gamma(\mathbb{P}^{n+1},\mathcal{O}(d))</math> this Hodge structure can be understood completely from the Jacobian ideal. For its graded-pieces, this is given by the map<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Introduction to Hodge theory|date=2002|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|author=José Bertin|isbn=0-8218-2040-0|location=Providence, R.I.|pages=199–205|oclc=48892689}}</ref><math display=block>\mathbb{C}[Z_0,\ldots, Z_n]^{(d(n-1+p) - (n+2))} \to \frac{F^pH^n(X,\mathbb{C})}{F^{p+1}H^n(X,\mathbb{C})}</math>which is surjective on the primitive cohomology, denoted <math>\text{Prim}^{p,n-p}(X)</math> and has the kernel <math>J_f</math>. Note the primitive cohomology classes are the classes of <math>X</math> which do not come from <math>\mathbb{P}^{n+1}</math>, which is just the Lefschetz class <math>[L]^n = c_1(\mathcal{O}(1))^d</math>.

=== Sketch of proof ===

==== Reduction to residue map ====
For <math>X \subset \mathbb{P}^{n+1}</math> there is an associated short [[exact sequence]] of complexes<math display="block">0 \to \Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}^\bullet \to \Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}^\bullet(\log X) \xrightarrow{res} \Omega_X^\bullet[-1] \to 0</math>where the middle complex is the complex of sheaves of [[logarithmic form]]s and the right-hand map is the [[Poincaré residue|residue map]]. This has an associated long exact sequence in cohomology. From the [[Lefschetz hyperplane theorem]] there is only one interesting cohomology group of <math>X</math>, which is <math>H^n(X;\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{H}^n(X;\Omega_X^\bullet)</math>. From the long exact sequence of this short exact sequence, there the induced residue map<math display=block>\mathbb{H}^{n+1}\left(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}, \Omega^\bullet_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}(\log X)\right) \to 
\mathbb{H}^{n+1}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1},\Omega^\bullet_X[-1])</math>where the right hand side is equal to <math>\mathbb{H}^{n}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1},\Omega^\bullet_X)</math>, which is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{H}^n(X;\Omega_X^\bullet)</math>. Also, there is an isomorphism <math display=block>H^{n+1}_{dR}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X) \cong \mathbb{H}^{n+1}\left(\mathbb{P}^{n+1};\Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}^\bullet(\log X)\right)</math>Through these isomorphisms there is an induced residue map<math display=block>res: H^{n+1}_{dR}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X) \to H^n(X;\mathbb{C})</math>which is injective, and surjective on primitive cohomology. Also, there is the Hodge decomposition<math display=block>H^{n+1}_{dR}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X) \cong
\bigoplus_{p+q = n+1}H^q(\Omega_{\mathbb{P}}^p(\log X))</math>and <math>H^q(\Omega_{\mathbb{P}}^p(\log X)) \cong \text{Prim}^{p-1,q}(X)</math>.

==== Computation of de Rham cohomology group ====
In turns out the [[de Rham cohomology]] group <math>H^{n+1}_{dR}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X)</math> is much more tractable and has an explicit description in terms of polynomials. The <math>F^p</math> part is spanned by the meromorphic forms having poles of order <math>\leq n - p + 1</math> which surjects onto the <math>F^p</math> part of <math>\text{Prim}^n(X)</math>. This comes from the reduction isomorphism<math display=block>F^{p+1}H^{n+1}_{dR}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X;\mathbb{C}) \cong \frac{
    \Gamma(\Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}(n-p+1))
}{
    d\Gamma(\Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n+1}}(n-p))
}</math>Using the canonical <math>(n+1)</math>-form<math display=block>\Omega = \sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j Z_j dZ_0\wedge \cdots \wedge \hat{dZ_j}\wedge \cdots \wedge dZ_{n+1}</math>on <math>\mathbb{P}^{n+1}</math> where the <math>\hat{dZ_j}</math> denotes the deletion from the index, these meromorphic differential forms look like<math display=block>\frac{A}{f^{n-p+1}}\Omega</math>where<math display=block>\begin{align}
\text{deg}(A) &= (n-p+1)\cdot\text{deg}(f) - \text{deg}(\Omega) \\
&= (n-p+1)\cdot d - (n + 2) \\
&= d(n-p+1) - (n+2)
\end{align}</math>Finally, it turns out the kernel<ref name=":0" /> <sup>Lemma 8.11</sup> is of all polynomials of the form <math>A' + fB</math> where <math>A' \in J_f</math>. Note the Euler identity<math display=block>f = \sum Z_j \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z_j}</math>shows <math>f \in J_f</math>.
